title: Mock 7 · Tough Numericals II
blurb: Final boss: calendar arbitrage, Sensex hedging, collars, butterflies with puts, bonus 2:3, expiry-day spread rules and multi-statement traps.

questions.q: The L.C. Gupta committee (report dated March 17, 1998) recommended that derivatives be declared as which of the following, so that the existing regulatory framework could govern them?
questions.explanation: The committee recommended that derivatives be declared 'securities' so that the regulatory framework for securities would also govern derivatives. SCRA was amended accordingly in 1999.
hints: Equity derivatives were not brought under commodity law.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed in the workbook as a factor driving the global growth of financial derivatives?
options: Increased fluctuations in underlying asset prices
questions.explanation: Growth drivers include price volatility, global market integration, technology lowering costs, better understanding of risk tools, and product innovation. No government guarantees returns.
hints: Correct choice: not a driver; no one guarantees derivative returns.

questions.q: A price-weighted index of 5 stocks stands at 510. One constituent rises by ₹50 while the others are unchanged. What is the new index value?
questions.explanation: A price index is the sum of prices divided by 5, so a ₹50 rise in one stock adds 50/5 = 10 points: 510 + 10 = 520.
hints: This forgets to divide by the number of stocks.

questions.q: An equal-weighted index of four stocks starts at 100. Over the period the stocks return +20%, −10%, +8% and +2%. What is the new index value?
questions.explanation: With equal 25% weights, index return = 0.25 × (20 − 10 + 8 + 2) = 5%. New value = 105.
hints: Arithmetic error in the weighted sum.
This uses only the best performer.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹200 and the interest rate is 9% p.a. (continuous). Near-month futures trade at ₹201.20 and next-month futures at ₹203.40. The fair prices are about ₹201.51 and ₹203.02. What calendar-spread arbitrage should be done?
options: Buy near-month futures and sell next-month futures
Sell near-month futures and buy next-month futures
No action; there is no mispricing
questions.explanation: The fair spread is about 1.52 but the actual spread is 2.20, so the next month is overpriced relative to the near month. Buy the underpriced near contract and sell the overpriced next contract, and unwind when the spread normalises.
hints: Correct: buy the relatively cheap near month and sell the relatively expensive next month.
That is the opposite trade, suited when the spread is too NARROW.
The actual spread of 2.20 is well above the fair spread of 1.52.

questions.q: An arbitrageur sells 300 shares at ₹100 and buys 300 shares' worth of one-month futures at ₹92. He invests the sale proceeds at 8% p.a. (continuous) for one month. Holding to expiry, what is his total gain?
hints: This ignores the interest earned on the proceeds.
This subtracts the interest instead of adding it.

questions.q: A trader buys 2 lots of Sensex futures (lot size 20) at 80,000. The daily settlement prices are 80,250 on Day 1 and 79,900 on Day 2. What is the MTM on Day 2?
questions.explanation: For Day 2 (a brought-forward position), MTM = (79,900 − 80,250) × 20 × 2 = −350 × 40 = −₹14,000.
hints: This measures from the trade price instead of the previous settlement price.

questions.q: A portfolio worth ₹50 lakh has a beta of 1.5. Sensex futures trade at 80,000 with a lot size of 20. How many contracts should be sold to hedge?
hints: A hedge for a long portfolio needs SHORT futures.

questions.q: An investor holding 800 shares shorts one lot (800) of futures at ₹455 to hedge a planned sale. On the sale date the spot is ₹420 and the futures are ₹421. What is his effective selling price per share?
hints: This subtracts the gain instead of adding it.
The basis shift makes it ₹454, not exactly 455.

questions.q: Consider: (I) The basis for a one-month contract differs from that of a two-month contract. (II) The difference between these bases should essentially equal the cost of carry between month 1 and month 2. (III) Basis is always negative for equity futures. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II follow from the workbook's explanation of basis. III is false: basis can turn positive or negative during the contract's life (e.g. backwardation), and it is zero at expiry.

questions.q: A trader buys a 1,000-strike call at ₹40 and sells a 1,000-strike put at ₹35 (same expiry). The stock settles at ₹940. What is his net P&L per share?
questions.explanation: Long call expires worthless: −40. Short put: 35 − (1,000 − 940) = −25. Net = −65. This combination behaves like long futures at about 1,005.
hints: This counts only the net premium.
This counts only the put leg.
Wrong sign on the put loss.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹1,000. Calls are quoted as: 900 strike @ ₹112, 950 @ ₹68, 1,000 @ ₹45 and 1,100 @ ₹12. Which call has the highest time value?
questions.explanation: Time values: 900 → 112 − 100 = 12; 950 → 68 − 50 = 18; 1,000 → 45 (all time value); 1,100 → 12. The ATM option has the highest time value because uncertainty is greatest.
hints: Correct: the ATM option has a time value of 45.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹500. The 480-strike call trades at ₹30 and the 480-strike put at ₹6. Which statement is correct?
options: The call has intrinsic value ₹30 and time value nil
The put is in the money with intrinsic value ₹20
Both options have only time value
The call has intrinsic value ₹20 and time value ₹10; the put has only time value of ₹6
questions.explanation: Call IV = 500 − 480 = 20 and TV = 30 − 20 = 10. The put is OTM (S > X), so IV = 0 and its whole ₹6 premium is time value.
hints: The put is OTM because S > X.

questions.q: Which statement about daily MTM correctly distinguishes futures from options?
options: In futures both buyer and seller are subject to daily MTM; in options only the seller is subject to MTM margins
In both futures and options, only the buyer pays MTM
In options, both buyer and seller pay MTM margins daily
Neither futures nor options are marked to market
questions.explanation: Futures buyers and sellers both pay or receive MTM daily. In options, only the seller is subject to MTM margins; the buyer's risk is capped at the premium paid.
hints: Buyers of options are not subject to MTM.
Option buyers are exempt from MTM margins.
Futures are settled daily by MTM.

questions.q: A trader buys 2 lots (lot size 65) of a Nifty 25,000 put at ₹150. What are his maximum possible loss and the total contract value (at strike) of the position?
questions.explanation: Max loss = premium = 150 × 65 × 2 = ₹19,500. Contract value = 25,000 × 65 × 2 = ₹32,50,000, so the premium is only about 0.6% of exposure (leverage).
hints: Mixed: the contract value counts only 1 lot.
A put buyer's loss is limited to the premium.

questions.q: A call has a delta of 0.50 and a gamma of 0.08. If the underlying FALLS by ₹1, the new delta is approximately:
questions.explanation: New delta = 0.50 + 0.08 × (−1) = 0.42. Gamma works in both directions.
hints: That is the delta after a RISE of ₹1.
Delta changes when the price moves.

questions.q: According to the workbook, how is a butterfly spread created using only put options?
options: Buy two middle-strike puts, sell one highest and one lowest strike put
Buy one highest-strike put and sell one lowest-strike put
Sell one put at each of three strikes
Buy one highest-strike put, sell two middle-strike puts, and buy one lowest-strike put
questions.explanation: With puts: buy one highest strike, sell two middle strikes and buy one lowest strike. The result is a limited-profit, limited-loss position.
hints: That is a bear put spread.

questions.q: An investor buys a stock at ₹950, sells a 1,000-strike call at ₹15 and buys a 900-strike put at ₹8. What is the net P&L per share if the stock settles at ₹860?
questions.explanation: Stock: 860 − 950 = −90. Short call expires worthless: +15. Long put: (900 − 860) − 8 = +32. Net = −90 + 15 + 32 = −₹43 (the collar's floor).
hints: This is the stock loss alone.

questions.q: A trader buys a 1,200 call at ₹45 and a 1,200 put at ₹38. What is his net P&L per share if the stock settles at ₹1,150?
questions.explanation: Put payoff = 50 − 38 = +12; the call expires worthless: −45. Net = −33. The lower BEP is 1,200 − 83 = 1,117, so the stock has not fallen far enough.
hints: That is the put leg only.
That is the maximum loss, at 1,200 only.
That is the gross put payoff.

questions.q: Futures prices are falling and open interest is rising. What does this indicate, and what do traders usually do?
options: Build-up of short positions (bearish); traders tend to go short
questions.explanation: A falling price with rising OI indicates a build-up of short positions and a bearish trend, so traders usually go short.
hints: Long unwinding = falling price with falling OI.
Short covering = rising price with falling OI.
Fresh longs = rising price with rising OI.

questions.q: An investor buys a stock at ₹720 and writes a 750-strike call at ₹14. What are the maximum profit and the break-even price of this covered call?
questions.explanation: Max profit = (750 − 720) + 14 = ₹44, earned at or above 750. BEP = 720 − 14 = ₹706.
hints: The premium lowers the BEP; it doesn't raise it.

questions.q: Under SEBI's revised dynamic price band rules, after a derivative-eligible stock's band has been flexed twice by 5%, what is the next flex?
questions.explanation: The first two increases are 5% after 15 minutes. The next two are 3% after 30 minutes. Further increases are 2% after 60 minutes.
hints: Only the first two flexes are 5%.
That applies from the fifth flex onwards.

questions.q: A company announces a bonus in the ratio 2:3 (A:B). A stock option has a strike of ₹1,500 and a lot size of 300. What are the adjusted strike and lot?
questions.explanation: Bonus AF = (A + B)/B = (2 + 3)/3 = 5/3. New strike = 1,500 ÷ 5/3 = ₹900; new lot = 300 × 5/3 = 500. Value is preserved (₹4,50,000).
hints: This uses A/B = 2/3, the split formula.

questions.q: Consider: (I) If a stock fails the continued eligibility criteria for three consecutive months, no fresh month contracts are issued on it. (II) Existing unexpired contracts may trade till expiry and new strikes may be introduced in them. (III) Once excluded, the stock cannot be re-included for one year. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: All three are stated in the workbook. Re-introduction also requires meeting the criteria for six consecutive months.
hints: II and III are also correct.

questions.q: Single-stock monthly expiries fall on the 29th (current), 30th (next) and 31st (far). Under SEBI's February 2026 circular (effective May 5, 2026), which calendar spreads get calendar-spread margin treatment on the 29th?
questions.explanation: Positions involving contracts expiring on that day (29th) lose the calendar-spread benefit. Spreads between the 30th and 31st continue to receive the treatment.
hints: Spreads involving the expiring contract lose the benefit.
This leg expires on the 29th, so it loses the benefit.

questions.q: A client is short one lot (400 shares) of a stock call with a strike of ₹1,150 and is assigned on expiry when the stock closes at ₹1,210. What is the client's settlement obligation?
questions.explanation: Stock options are physically settled at the strike price. An assigned short call is a sell obligation: deliver 400 shares and receive 1,150 × 400 = ₹4,60,000 on T+1.
hints: Cash settlement applies to index options.
That is the obligation of an exercised long call.
The settlement value uses the strike price, not the closing price.

questions.q: For an FPI Category II investor who is an individual, family office or corporate, the position limit in index futures (gross notional) is the higher of:
options: 15% of index futures OI or ₹500 crore
10% of index futures OI or ₹500 crore
5% of index futures OI or ₹500 crore
questions.explanation: FPI Cat I, MFs, TM proprietary and clients: higher of 15% or ₹500 crore. FPI Cat II (others): 10% or ₹500 crore. FPI Cat II individuals, family offices and corporates: 5% or ₹500 crore.
hints: Applies to FPI Cat I, MFs, TM prop and clients.
Applies to other FPI Cat II investors.

questions.q: A stock exchange suffers an outage and normal trading does not resume until 45 minutes before the scheduled close. As per SEBI's SOP, what happens?
options: Only the affected exchange extends trading by 30 minutes
All stock exchanges extend trading hours by one and a half hours that day
Trading is cancelled for the day
questions.explanation: If trading does not resume at least 1 hour before the scheduled close, all stock exchanges extend trading hours by 1.5 hours that day.
hints: No change applies only if trading resumes at least 1 hour before close.
The extension applies to all exchanges and is 1.5 hours.
The SOP extends trading rather than cancelling it.

questions.q: A trader's F&O turnover for the year is ₹12 crore. As per the workbook, a tax audit is:
options: Not required if more than 95% of transactions are digital
Required only if profits are below 6% of turnover
Mandatory regardless of profit or loss, under Section 44AB(a)
questions.explanation: A tax audit is mandatory if turnover exceeds ₹10 crore, regardless of profit or loss. The digital-transactions and 6% conditions apply only to turnover between ₹2 crore and ₹10 crore.
hints: The 95%-digital exemption applies only to turnover of ₹2–10 crore.
The 6% test applies only to turnover of ₹2–10 crore.

questions.q: In which situation is in-person verification NOT required when opening a trading or demat account?
options: When KYC is completed using Aadhaar authentication of UIDAI
When the client is a high net-worth individual
When the client is a non-resident
When the broker's branch is in the same city as the client
questions.explanation: IPV is compulsory, except when KYC is done through Aadhaar authentication/verification, or the form is submitted online with documents via DigiLocker or another source verifiable online.
hints: HNIs are clients of special category; IPV still applies.
NRIs are clients of special category; IPV still applies.
